title: Collatz Cycles OQ-04: The Algebraic Cycle Product Equation
description: Formalizes the algebraic cycle product equation: for any Collatz cycle with j odd elements n₁,...,nⱼ and mᵢ halvings after the i-th odd step, ∏(3nᵢ+1) = 2^M · ∏nᵢ where M = Σmᵢ. This identity is the algebraic heart of Collatz cycle theory — it immediately implies the halving constraint 2^M > 3^j and underlies Eliahou's lower bound on cycle length.

meta.author: Lean Genius
meta.assumptions: 2 sorries: (1) collatz_cycle_halving_constraint — proof outlined via product equation, routine cancellation; (2) collatz_cycle_additive_eq — proof by induction on j, unfurling cycle equations.
originalContributions: cyclicSucc/cyclicPred: cyclic successor and predecessor on Fin j with mutual-inverse proofs
collatz_cycle_product_eq: ∏(3ns+1) = 2^M · ∏ns for any Collatz cycle (proved via cyclic bijection on products)
collatz_one_odd_step: characterization that n=1, m=2 is the unique 1-odd-step solution to 3n+1 = 2^m·n
cycleForcingSum: definition of the additive forcing sum S(ms) = Σₖ 3^(j-1-k)·2^(Σᵢ≤ₖ ms(i))

mathlibDependencies.description: Reindexing a product via a bijection on the index set

overview.historicalContext: The Collatz conjecture (n → n/2 or 3n+1) was introduced by Lothar Collatz in 1937. A key approach to understanding cycles is algebraic: any cycle must satisfy the 'cycle product equation' ∏(3nᵢ+1) = 2^M·∏nᵢ. This identity was implicit in Lagarias (1985) and made central to Eliahou's 1993 lower bound on cycle lengths (any non-trivial cycle has length ≥ 17,087,915). The halving constraint 2^M > 3^j, previously proved by case analysis on j, follows immediately from this product equation.
overview.problemStatement:
Given a Collatz cycle visiting odd elements n₁,...,nⱼ with mᵢ halvings after each odd step (so 3nᵢ+1 = 2^mᵢ·nᵢ₊₁ for each i, indices mod j), prove the **cycle product equation**:

  ∏ᵢ (3nᵢ + 1) = 2^M · ∏ᵢ nᵢ,   where M = Σᵢ mᵢ
overview.proofStrategy: Take the product of all j step equations: ∏(3nᵢ+1) = ∏(2^mᵢ·nᵢ₊₁). Split: = (∏2^mᵢ)·(∏nᵢ₊₁). Use ∏2^mᵢ = 2^(Σmᵢ) = 2^M. The key step: ∏nᵢ₊₁ = ∏nᵢ because i ↦ (i+1 mod j) is a permutation of {0,...,j-1}, and products are invariant under reindexing by bijections. In Lean, this uses `Finset.prod_nbij` with the cyclic successor map.
keyInsights: The cyclic successor i ↦ (i+1) mod j is a bijection on Fin j, so ∏nᵢ₊₁ = ∏nᵢ — products are invariant under permutations of the index set
∏2^mᵢ = 2^(Σmᵢ) by the 'product of powers = power of sum' identity (Finset.prod_pow_eq_pow_sum)
The halving constraint 2^M > 3^j follows in two lines from the product equation: since 3n+1 > 3n for each positive odd n, the LHS product exceeds the RHS by a factor strictly greater than 1
The additive form (2^M - 3^j)·n₁ = S(ms) determines the smallest cycle element from the halving sequence alone, and is the key to Eliahou's quantitative bounds
prerequisites: Finset products and the prod_nbij reindexing lemma

conclusion.summary: This formalization proves the cycle product equation ∏(3nᵢ+1) = 2^M·∏nᵢ for Collatz cycles, with key infrastructure including the cyclic bijection on Fin j and the one-odd-step characterization. Two sorries remain: the halving constraint corollary (2^M > 3^j, proof outlined) and the additive cycle equation (by induction).
conclusion.implications: The product equation is the algebraic foundation for all quantitative Collatz cycle results. It gives a 3-line proof of the halving constraint that was previously only available via case analysis. The additive form leads directly to lower bounds on cycle element magnitudes.
openQuestions: Complete the halving constraint proof from the product equation (straightforward cancellation)
Complete the additive cycle equation by induction on j (then Eliahou's bound follows)
Use the forcing sum to formalize Eliahou's result: any non-trivial cycle has length ≥ 17,087,915

sections.title: Part I: Cyclic Successor on Fin j
sections.summary: Defines cyclicSucc (i ↦ (i+1)%j) and cyclicPred (i ↦ (i+j-1)%j) on Fin j, proves they are mutual inverses via omega, establishing the cyclic permutation structure needed for the product reindexing.

sections.title: Part II: The Cycle Product Equation
sections.summary: collatz_cycle_product_eq: the main theorem. Proof: simp_rw the step equations, split the product, apply prod_pow_eq_pow_sum for the exponential factor, then prod_nbij with cyclicSucc for the bijective reindexing of ∏nᵢ₊₁ = ∏nᵢ.

sections.title: Part III: The Halving Constraint
sections.summary: collatz_cycle_halving_constraint (sorry): outlines how 2^M > 3^j follows from the product equation + strict inequality 3n+1 > 3n. Subsumes the case-by-case proof in CollatzCycles.lean.

sections.title: Part IV: The Unique One-Odd-Step Cycle
sections.summary: collatz_one_odd_step: if 3n+1 = 2^m·n with n positive odd, then n=1 and m=2. Proof: m ≥ 2 by case analysis, then (2^m-3)·n = 1 forces both factors to be 1, giving n=1 and 2^m=4 hence m=2.

sections.title: Part V: Additive Cycle Equation
sections.summary: cycleForcingSum definition and collatz_cycle_additive_eq (sorry): the relationship (2^M-3^j)·n₁ = S(ms) that characterizes cycles and enables Eliahou-type lower bounds.
